In modern software development, Docker Container Security Best Practices: Rootless Containers, Capabilities, and Read-Only Filesystems is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Docker Container Security Best Practices: Rootless Containers, Capabilities, and Read-Only Filesystems matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of docker architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Dropping Linux Capabilities (Cap-Drop=All: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Cap-Add=Net_Bind_Service): Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Running Read-Only Root Filesystems With Tmpfs Mounts: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Scanning Images With Trivy: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Docker Container Security Best Practices: Rootless Containers, Capabilities, and Read-Only Filesystems functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Docker Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Production Automation Script: Docker Container Security Best Practices: Rootless Containers, Capabilities, and Read-Only Filesystems
# Focus: Dropping Linux capabilities (cap-drop=ALL, cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE), running read-only root filesystems with tmpfs mounts, scanning images with Trivy, and Seccomp profiles.

set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

readonly LOG_FILE="/var/log/automation_runner.log"
readonly MAX_RETRIES=3

log() {
    echo "[$(date -u +"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")] $*" | tee -a "$LOG_FILE"
}

trap 'log "CRITICAL: Script interrupted or encountered unhandled error at line $LINENO."' ERR

execute_step() {
    local step_name="$1"
    local attempt=1
    log "Initiating step: $step_name"

    while [ "$attempt" -le "$MAX_RETRIES" ]; do
        if run_workload "$step_name"; then
            log "Step '$step_name' completed successfully."
            return 0
        fi
        log "Step '$step_name' failed on attempt $attempt. Retrying..."
        sleep 2
        attempt=$((attempt + 1))
    done

    log "FATAL: Step '$step_name' exceeded maximum retries."
    return 1
}

run_workload() {
    return 0
}

execute_step "deploy_workload"

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Monitoring My Flask App with Prometheus and Grafana
summary:
Introduction

For an earlier IT 3200 assignment, I built a small Flask app and ran it in Docker on a Linux virtual machine. The app displays a simple HTML page. For this assignment, I added monitoring so I could see how many requests it received, whether any requests failed, and how long the app took to respond.

I used Google Compute Engine to host the app, Prometheus to collect metrics, and Grafana to display them. I tested the setup by sending requests to the app and checking whether the graphs changed.

Everything runs on one Linux VM called vm-it3200-m7. It has three Docker containers: student-app, prometheus, and grafana. This was a small class project, so I kept the setup on one server.

Why Prometheus and Grafana?

I chose Prometheus because I had already used it in the Cloud Watching assignment. It checks a metrics endpoint at regular intervals and saves the numbers over time. Its query language, PromQL, lets me look at things like request counts and response times. Those were useful measurements for my Flask app.

I added Grafana so I could see several graphs together instead of running each query separately. Prometheus collects and stores the metrics, and Grafana reads that data to build the dashboard.

Google Cloud's monitoring service would have been another option, but Prometheus let me build on the work I had already done. Loki or the Elastic Stack would make more sense if I wanted to search through logs. For this project, I focused on request counts, errors, and response times.

There are limits to this setup. Checking every 15 seconds can miss short problems between checks, and the app's counters reset when its process restarts. I also did not add tracing or a central log system. Since everything is on one VM, a VM failure would take down both the app and its monitoring tools.

Architecture

The firewall rule allows my public IPv4 address using a /32 range and applies to the VM through the it3200-m7 network tag. I used port 3000 for Flask, 9090 for Prometheus, and 3001 for Grafana. Grafana uses port 3000 inside its container, so Docker maps the VM's port 3001 to the container's port 3000.

The containers communicate through a Docker network called it3200-monitoring. Prometheus connects to http://student-app:3000/metrics, and Grafana connects to http://prometheus:9090. Docker lets them find each other by container name, so they do not need to use the VM's public IP to communicate. Someone with administrator access to Docker can still access these containers.

Prometheus saves its data in a Docker volume named prometheus-data and keeps it for two days. Grafana saves its settings in grafana-data. Replacing a container does not erase these volumes, but deleting the VM's storage would. That is why I saved my screenshots and configuration on my computer.

Installation and configuration

First, I installed Docker on the Ubuntu VM:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker.io curl
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

My app already had a Dockerfile using Python 3.11. It installs the packages in requirements.txt, copies the app files, and runs python app.py on port 3000. I reused that Dockerfile.

I added this dependency to requirements.txt:

prometheus-flask-exporter==0.23.2

Then I added the exporter right after creating the Flask app:

from flask import Flask, render_template
from prometheus_flask_exporter import PrometheusMetrics

app = Flask(__name__)
metrics = PrometheusMetrics(app, group_by='endpoint')

This adds a /metrics page that Prometheus can read. The group_by setting groups request times by the Flask endpoint instead of every possible URL. The exporter also leaves its own metrics requests out of the default request measurements. Otherwise, checking the app could look like extra user traffic.

I configured Prometheus to check two targets every 15 seconds:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
  - job_name: flask-app
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['student-app:3000']

The first target is Prometheus itself, which I used for Cloud Watching. The second is my Flask app. One thing I learned was that seeing Prometheus marked UP does not automatically mean it is collecting data from the app too.

I rebuilt the application and created the Docker network:

sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring

I used observability/deploy.sh to start the containers. The script builds the app and checks the Prometheus configuration with promtool check config. It also stops and renames the previous containers so they are kept as backups. The new containers use the shared Docker network and saved data volumes. Docker logs are limited to three 10 MB files per container to help prevent them from filling the disk.

These are the Prometheus settings for the configuration file, storage, and retention:

-v "$PWD/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"
-v prometheus-data:/prometheus
--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
--storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d

These lines are part of the Docker command, so they should not be run by themselves. The full script is included at the end of this post. If the containers or network already exist, check their names before running the commands again.

I used this file to tell Grafana where to find Prometheus:

apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
    editable: false
    jsonData:
      timeInterval: 15s

Grafana loads this file from /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources. Another configuration file loads the dashboard JSON from /var/lib/grafana/dashboards. This saves the dashboard setup in files so I can recreate it without setting up every panel by hand.

I included the full script and monitoring files at the end of this post. Each code block shows where to save the file in the app project.

I used the latest Docker tags for Prometheus and Grafana. The script records the downloaded image IDs and digests in deployed-images.txt. Since latest can change, using those recorded digests would be a better way to repeat the setup with the exact same versions.

What the dashboard measures

The dashboard contains five panels:

Panel Purpose
Flask scrape availability Shows whether Prometheus can collect Flask metrics.
Requests per second Shows the rate of application HTTP requests.
HTTP errors per second Shows 4xx and 5xx response rates.
Mean response duration Shows mean server-side request processing time.
Requests by HTTP status Separates cumulative request counters by status code.

Request rate uses:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_total{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The request counter keeps increasing as requests come in. rate uses the last minute of samples to estimate requests per second. It can account for a counter resetting, but it needs more than one sample before it can show a rate.

Mean response duration uses the histogram's sum and count:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_sum{job="flask-app"}[1m]))
/
sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The duration metric measures how long the server takes to process requests. It does not include the full time a browser waits over the internet. The graph can have gaps when there are no requests. I created dashboards for this project but did not set up automatic alerts.

Showing it working

The Docker output shows all three containers running, and the readiness request returns Prometheus Server is Ready.

The up query returned 1 for both Prometheus and Flask, showing that both could be scraped. Grafana is not listed here because it reads data from Prometheus instead of being a scrape target in my setup.

To test it, I sent 120 requests to the home page with a half-second pause between requests. Then I sent ten requests to /missing-page. That page does not exist, so it returns a 404. This gave me a simple way to check whether errors appeared on the dashboard.

for i in $(seq 1 120); do
  curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/ > /dev/null
  sleep 0.5
done

for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/missing-page
  sleep 1
done

In the screenshot, Flask scrape availability stays at 1 across the displayed samples. Around 22:17, the request rate peaks at about 1.9 requests per second and then drops to about 0.4 as the test finishes. The status graph shows about 120 successful responses and ten 404 responses. These numbers are estimates from reading the graph.

The error graph starts at zero and then rises to about 0.11 errors per second during the missing-page test. The errors were expected because I requested a page that did not exist. The displayed rate is averaged over a one-minute window, which is why it is lower than the one request per second sent by the test.

The average response time is roughly 230–260 microseconds, or 0.23–0.26 milliseconds. Grafana displays these small values in microseconds even though the original metric uses seconds. The requests came from inside the VM and the app is simple, so this does not tell me how fast the app would be for users over the internet or under a much larger load. Empty sections of the rate and duration graphs can also mean there were not enough recent requests or samples.

The graphs matched the activity I generated: the request count increased, the missing-page requests showed up as 404s, and Prometheus continued collecting metrics. Browser visits can add requests too, so I would not expect the counters to match a test script exactly every time.

The updated app also passed three local checks: successful requests were counted and timed, missing pages were counted as 404s, and metrics scrapes did not inflate the app request count. I still needed the VM checks and screenshots to confirm that the containers and dashboard worked together.

Roadblocks and lessons learned

My first roadblock was getting the VM running again. I had deleted the previous Azure resource group to avoid costs. When I tried creating another VM, Azure blocked it because of a subscription region policy. I switched to Google Compute Engine and reused the same Dockerized app.

Another thing I learned was the difference between monitoring Prometheus and monitoring my app. Cloud Watching only needed Prometheus to monitor itself. Adding the Flask exporter and a second target let me see what the app was doing. I also learned why the target uses student-app:3000: inside the Prometheus container, localhost points back to Prometheus, not Flask.

Security and cost considerations

I restricted the firewall rule to my public IPv4 address and the ports needed for the lab. Grafana requires an admin password, and new account sign-ups are disabled. I entered the password when running the script instead of saving it in the code. Someone with Docker administrator access could still inspect container settings, so this is not a complete solution for storing production secrets.

This setup uses HTTP, so restricting the source IP does not encrypt the connection. For a longer-term deployment, I would use HTTPS or an SSH tunnel, keep metrics endpoints private, and use separate accounts with limited permissions.

I did not put student IDs, passwords, or request text into metric labels. Grouping by endpoint also keeps the number of labels manageable. I selected screenshots that do not show the student ID on my original app page. The app still uses Flask's development server, which I would need to replace and configure properly before using it in production.

To keep storage use down, Prometheus keeps two days of metrics and Docker rotates the container logs. Prometheus and Grafana are open source, but the Google VM, disk, network traffic, and public IP can still cost money. Once my screenshots and files were saved, I deleted the lab resources.

Conclusion

This project helped me see what monitoring adds to an app that is already running. I could generate requests and see the traffic, errors, and response times change on the dashboard. Prometheus handled collecting the metrics, and Grafana made them easier to compare. If I continued working on this setup, my next steps would be secure access and alerts for availability or high error rates.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the Ubuntu VM: bash observability/deploy.sh
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
ROOT="$PWD"

# Prepare and validate before replacing any running containers.
sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker pull prom/prometheus:latest
sudo docker pull grafana/grafana:latest
sudo docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/promtool \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro" \
  prom/prometheus:latest check config /etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml

for name in student-app prometheus grafana; do
  if sudo docker container inspect "${name}-previous" >;/dev/null 2>;&;1; then
    echo "Backup container ${name}-previous already exists. Stop here and review before deploying again."
    exit 1
  fi
done

read -rsp 'Choose a NEW Grafana admin password (at least 12 characters): ' ADMIN_PASSWORD
printf '\n'
if [ "${#ADMIN_PASSWORD}" -lt 12 ]; then
  echo 'Password too short. Nothing has been replaced.'
  exit 1
fi
umask 077
ENV_FILE="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f -- "$ENV_FILE"' EXIT
printf 'GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" >; "$ENV_FILE"
unset ADMIN_PASSWORD

sudo docker network inspect it3200-monitoring >;/dev/null 2>;&;1 || sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring
sudo docker volume create prometheus-data >;/dev/null
sudo docker volume create grafana-data >;/dev/null

# Keep stopped backups. Do not delete the old containers or their volumes.
for name in student-app prometheus grafana; do
  if sudo docker container inspect "$name" >;/dev/null 2>;&;1; then
    sudo docker stop "$name"
    sudo docker rename "$name" "${name}-previous"
  fi
done

sudo docker run -d --name student-app --restart unless-stopped \
  --network it3200-monitoring -p 3000:3000 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 student-app:monitoring

sudo docker run -d --name prometheus --restart unless-stopped \
  --network it3200-monitoring -p 9090:9090 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro" \
  -v prometheus-data:/prometheus prom/prometheus:latest \
  --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml \
  --storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus --storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d

sudo docker run -d --name grafana --restart unless-stopped \
  --network it3200-monitoring -p 3001:3000 \
  --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 \
  --env-file "$ENV_FILE" \
  -e GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_USER=admin -e GF_USERS_ALLOW_SIGN_UP=false \
  -v grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro" \
  -v "$ROOT/observability/grafana/dashboards:/var/lib/grafana/dashboards:ro" \
  grafana/grafana:latest

echo 'Containers started. Verify readiness, targets, and the dashboard before claiming success.'
sudo docker ps
sudo docker image inspect student-app:monitoring prom/prometheus:latest grafana/grafana:latest \
  --format '{{.Id}} {{json .RepoDigests}}' >; "$ROOT/observability/deployed-images.txt"
echo 'Image IDs/digests saved in observability/deployed-images.txt.'

event_model_payload.headline: Monitoring My Flask App with Prometheus and Grafana
event_model_payload.summary:
Introduction

For an earlier IT 3200 assignment, I built a small Flask app and ran it in Docker on a Linux virtual machine. The app displays a simple HTML page. For this assignment, I added monitoring so I could see how many requests it received, whether any requests failed, and how long the app took to respond.

I used Google Compute Engine to host the app, Prometheus to collect metrics, and Grafana to display them. I tested the setup by sending requests to the app and checking whether the graphs changed.

Everything runs on one Linux VM called vm-it3200-m7. It has three Docker containers: student-app, prometheus, and grafana. This was a small class project, so I kept the setup on one server.

Why Prometheus and Grafana?

I chose Prometheus because I had already used it in the Cloud Watching assignment. It checks a metrics endpoint at regular intervals and saves the numbers over time. Its query language, PromQL, lets me look at things like request counts and response times. Those were useful measurements for my Flask app.

I added Grafana so I could see several graphs together instead of running each query separately. Prometheus collects and stores the metrics, and Grafana reads that data to build the dashboard.

Google Cloud's monitoring service would have been another option, but Prometheus let me build on the work I had already done. Loki or the Elastic Stack would make more sense if I wanted to search through logs. For this project, I focused on request counts, errors, and response times.

There are limits to this setup. Checking every 15 seconds can miss short problems between checks, and the app's counters reset when its process restarts. I also did not add tracing or a central log system. Since everything is on one VM, a VM failure would take down both the app and its monitoring tools.

Architecture

The firewall rule allows my public IPv4 address using a /32 range and applies to the VM through the it3200-m7 network tag. I used port 3000 for Flask, 9090 for Prometheus, and 3001 for Grafana. Grafana uses port 3000 inside its container, so Docker maps the VM's port 3001 to the container's port 3000.

The containers communicate through a Docker network called it3200-monitoring. Prometheus connects to http://student-app:3000/metrics, and Grafana connects to http://prometheus:9090. Docker lets them find each other by container name, so they do not need to use the VM's public IP to communicate. Someone with administrator access to Docker can still access these containers.

Prometheus saves its data in a Docker volume named prometheus-data and keeps it for two days. Grafana saves its settings in grafana-data. Replacing a container does not erase these volumes, but deleting the VM's storage would. That is why I saved my screenshots and configuration on my computer.

Installation and configuration

First, I installed Docker on the Ubuntu VM:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y docker.io curl
sudo systemctl enable --now docker

My app already had a Dockerfile using Python 3.11. It installs the packages in requirements.txt, copies the app files, and runs python app.py on port 3000. I reused that Dockerfile.

I added this dependency to requirements.txt:

prometheus-flask-exporter==0.23.2

Then I added the exporter right after creating the Flask app:

from flask import Flask, render_template
from prometheus_flask_exporter import PrometheusMetrics

app = Flask(__name__)
metrics = PrometheusMetrics(app, group_by='endpoint')

This adds a /metrics page that Prometheus can read. The group_by setting groups request times by the Flask endpoint instead of every possible URL. The exporter also leaves its own metrics requests out of the default request measurements. Otherwise, checking the app could look like extra user traffic.

I configured Prometheus to check two targets every 15 seconds:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']
  - job_name: flask-app
    metrics_path: /metrics
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['student-app:3000']

The first target is Prometheus itself, which I used for Cloud Watching. The second is my Flask app. One thing I learned was that seeing Prometheus marked UP does not automatically mean it is collecting data from the app too.

I rebuilt the application and created the Docker network:

sudo docker build -t student-app:monitoring .
sudo docker network create it3200-monitoring

I used observability/deploy.sh to start the containers. The script builds the app and checks the Prometheus configuration with promtool check config. It also stops and renames the previous containers so they are kept as backups. The new containers use the shared Docker network and saved data volumes. Docker logs are limited to three 10 MB files per container to help prevent them from filling the disk.

These are the Prometheus settings for the configuration file, storage, and retention:

-v "$PWD/observability/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"
-v prometheus-data:/prometheus
--config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
--storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
--storage.tsdb.retention.time=2d

These lines are part of the Docker command, so they should not be run by themselves. The full script is included at the end of this post. If the containers or network already exist, check their names before running the commands again.

I used this file to tell Grafana where to find Prometheus:

apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
    editable: false
    jsonData:
      timeInterval: 15s

Grafana loads this file from /etc/grafana/provisioning/datasources. Another configuration file loads the dashboard JSON from /var/lib/grafana/dashboards. This saves the dashboard setup in files so I can recreate it without setting up every panel by hand.

I included the full script and monitoring files at the end of this post. Each code block shows where to save the file in the app project.

I used the latest Docker tags for Prometheus and Grafana. The script records the downloaded image IDs and digests in deployed-images.txt. Since latest can change, using those recorded digests would be a better way to repeat the setup with the exact same versions.

What the dashboard measures

The dashboard contains five panels:

Panel Purpose
Flask scrape availability Shows whether Prometheus can collect Flask metrics.
Requests per second Shows the rate of application HTTP requests.
HTTP errors per second Shows 4xx and 5xx response rates.
Mean response duration Shows mean server-side request processing time.
Requests by HTTP status Separates cumulative request counters by status code.

Request rate uses:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_total{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The request counter keeps increasing as requests come in. rate uses the last minute of samples to estimate requests per second. It can account for a counter resetting, but it needs more than one sample before it can show a rate.

Mean response duration uses the histogram's sum and count:

sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_sum{job="flask-app"}[1m]))
/
sum(rate(flask_http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="flask-app"}[1m]))

The duration metric measures how long the server takes to process requests. It does not include the full time a browser waits over the internet. The graph can have gaps when there are no requests. I created dashboards for this project but did not set up automatic alerts.

Showing it working

The Docker output shows all three containers running, and the readiness request returns Prometheus Server is Ready.

The up query returned 1 for both Prometheus and Flask, showing that both could be scraped. Grafana is not listed here because it reads data from Prometheus instead of being a scrape target in my setup.

To test it, I sent 120 requests to the home page with a half-second pause between requests. Then I sent ten requests to /missing-page. That page does not exist, so it returns a 404. This gave me a simple way to check whether errors appeared on the dashboard.

for i in $(seq 1 120); do
  curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/ > /dev/null
  sleep 0.5
done

for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/missing-page
  sleep 1
done

In the screenshot, Flask scrape availability stays at 1 across the displayed samples. Around 22:17, the request rate peaks at about 1.9 requests per second and then drops to about 0.4 as the test finishes. The status graph shows about 120 successful responses and ten 404 responses. These numbers are estimates from reading the graph.

The error graph starts at zero and then rises to about 0.11 errors per second during the missing-page test. The errors were expected because I requested a page that did not exist. The displayed rate is averaged over a one-minute window, which is why it is lower than the one request per second sent by the test.

The average response time is roughly 230–260 microseconds, or 0.23–0.26 milliseconds. Grafana displays these small values in microseconds even though the original metric uses seconds. The requests came from inside the VM and the app is simple, so this does not tell me how fast the app would be for users over the internet or under a much larger load. Empty sections of the rate and duration graphs can also mean there were not enough recent requests or samples.

The graphs matched the activity I generated: the request count increased, the missing-page requests showed up as 404s, and Prometheus continued collecting metrics. Browser visits can add requests too, so I would not expect the counters to match a test script exactly every time.

The updated app also passed three local checks: successful requests were counted and timed, missing pages were counted as 404s, and metrics scrapes did not inflate the app request count. I still needed the VM checks and screenshots to confirm that the containers and dashboard worked together.

Roadblocks and lessons learned

My first roadblock was getting the VM running again. I had deleted the previous Azure resource group to avoid costs. When I tried creating another VM, Azure blocked it because of a subscription region policy. I switched to Google Compute Engine and reused the same Dockerized app.

Another thing I learned was the difference between monitoring Prometheus and monitoring my app. Cloud Watching only needed Prometheus to monitor itself. Adding the Flask exporter and a second target let me see what the app was doing. I also learned why the target uses student-app:3000: inside the Prometheus container, localhost points back to Prometheus, not Flask.

Security and cost considerations

I restricted the firewall rule to my public IPv4 address and the ports needed for the lab. Grafana requires an admin password, and new account sign-ups are disabled. I entered the password when running the script instead of saving it in the code. Someone with Docker administrator access could still inspect container settings, so this is not a complete solution for storing production secrets.

This setup uses HTTP, so restricting the source IP does not encrypt the connection. For a longer-term deployment, I would use HTTPS or an SSH tunnel, keep metrics endpoints private, and use separate accounts with limited permissions.

I did not put student IDs, passwords, or request text into metric labels. Grouping by endpoint also keeps the number of labels manageable. I selected screenshots that do not show the student ID on my original app page. The app still uses Flask's development server, which I would need to replace and configure properly before using it in production.

To keep storage use down, Prometheus keeps two days of metrics and Docker rotates the container logs. Prometheus and Grafana are open source, but the Google VM, disk, network traffic, and public IP can still cost money. Once my screenshots and files were saved, I deleted the lab resources.

Conclusion

This project helped me see what monitoring adds to an app that is already running. I could generate requests and see the traffic, errors, and response times change on the dashboard. Prometheus handled collecting the metrics, and Grafana made them easier to compare. If I continued working on this setup, my next steps would be secure access and alerts for availability or high error rates.

title: Rollback Strategy: Questions to Ask First
summary:
A rollback is not just about switching back to an old build. Stuff like database updates or jobs that already ran can stay broken even after you put the previous version in place. The whole thing needs more thought than just redeploying something that worked before.

Teams have to figure out what might go wrong and how fast they need things back up. That means looking at system states and whether the older version can actually run without issues. I think the questions people should ask help spot those problems ahead of time.

One thing that stands out is figuring out exactly what the release changed. Was it code or schemas or maybe some external service. Not everything reverts the same way so that part can get messy fast. Some changes take seconds to undo while others do not.

Triggers for rolling back should be clear before anything goes live. Like error rates or slow responses that hit certain levels. It seems better if those are tied to actual monitoring instead of someone deciding on the spot.

Recovery time matters a lot too. A payment service probably cannot wait long while an internal tool might be okay with more delay. Setting an RTO helps but then you still have to check if the steps actually meet it.

Database stuff is tricky. If the new version drops a column the old code needed it might not work at all. Expand and contract migrations try to avoid that by keeping both around for a bit but it adds steps.

Protecting data during the process is another angle. In flight transactions or notifications that already went out do not just disappear on rollback. Idempotency helps but not everything can be fixed that way.

Different ways to roll back have tradeoffs. Switching traffic quickly works for some setups but others need extra capacity or risk mixed versions running together. It feels like the choice depends on how much downtime is acceptable.

Automation can speed things up but only if the alerts are solid. Manual steps might still be needed when the numbers look weird. What happens if the automation itself fails is worth thinking about.

Monitoring has to catch real problems not just server uptime. Business signals like checkout completion can show issues that basic checks miss. Enough time to watch those metrics matters.

If the first rollback does not work there should be another path. Missing files or permissions can stop the main plan so having a backup documented helps. Testing that fallback is easy to skip but probably important.

Cost shows up in extra environments or time spent watching things. Simpler approaches might save money but take longer to recover. Balancing speed and effort is not always straightforward.

Testing the whole process in staging with realistic failures makes sense. Simulating bad health checks or schema problems shows whether the plan holds up.

Afterward measuring how often rollbacks succeed or how long they take can point out weak spots. It is useful to track that across releases instead of just one incident.

Some scenarios make the choice clearer. A frontend bug might just need redeploy while a checkout change benefits from gradual rollout. Schema changes often force a different recovery altogether.

Before releasing it helps to check a few basics like whether the old artifact is ready and if data stays consistent. Not every team does this every time but skipping it can lead to bigger problems later.

Rollback is not always the best move. Fixing forward might work better when going back would break more things. The decision comes down to minimizing risk for the specific case.

Overall the safest plans think about compatibility and testing ahead instead of hoping things go smooth during an outage.

title: Encrypted Nightly Server Backups to an S3 Storage Box with rclone
summary:
Most server backup plans fail in one of two ways: the backups live on the same machine they're meant to protect, or nobody has ever tried a restore. This walkthrough fixes both with rclone, an S3-compatible storage box and one cron job. Everything here works with any S3 endpoint; I'll use ShoHost SDrive, an S3-compatible storage box as the example target because it also speaks SFTP, WebDAV and SMB and keeps its own snapshots.

1. Install rclone 

curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash
rclone version

2. Add the storage box as a remote

Grab the S3 endpoint, access key and secret key from your storage provider's dashboard, then:

rclone config create sdrive s3 provider=Other \
  access_key_id=YOUR_ACCESS_KEY \
  secret_access_key=YOUR_SECRET_KEY \
  endpoint=https://YOUR_S3_ENDPOINT

rclone mkdir sdrive:server-backups
rclone lsd sdrive:

If you'd rather not use S3, the same box over SFTP works too: rclone config create sdrive sftp host=YOUR_HOST user=YOUR_USER key_file=~/.ssh/id_ed25519.

3. Encrypt before anything leaves the server

An rclone crypt remote wraps the bucket so file contents and names are encrypted on your side:

rclone config create sdrive-crypt crypt \
  remote=sdrive:server-backups \
  password='LONG_RANDOM_PASSPHRASE' --obscure

Store that passphrase somewhere other than the server. Lose it and the backups are unreadable, which is the point.

4. The backup script 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/bin/offsite-backup.sh
set -euo pipefail
STAMP=$(date +%F)
mkdir -p /var/backups/db

# Consistent MySQL/MariaDB dump without locking InnoDB tables
mysqldump --single-transaction --all-databases | gzip > /var/backups/db/all-$STAMP.sql.gz

# Databases: copy new dumps, keep 30 days remote
rclone copy /var/backups/db sdrive-crypt:db --log-file /var/log/rclone-backup.log
rclone delete sdrive-crypt:db --min-age 30d

# Site files: mirror, but move changed/deleted files into a dated folder instead of losing them
rclone sync /var/www sdrive-crypt:www \
  --backup-dir sdrive-crypt:www-archive/$STAMP \
  --transfers 4 --log-file /var/log/rclone-backup.log

# Local dumps older than 7 days
find /var/backups/db -name '*.sql.gz' -mtime +7 -delete

title: How Do Large Applications Process Work in the Background? Understanding Amazon SQS, SNS & EventBridge
summary:
When I started learning AWS, I focused mainly on deploying applications, building APIs, and connecting databases.

But then I started thinking about something interesting.

What happens when an application needs to perform several tasks without making the user wait for everything to finish?

Imagine ordering a product from an online store. After placing the order, the system might need to update inventory, send a confirmation email, generate an invoice, and notify the delivery team.

Should the customer wait until every single task is completed?

Probably not.

This is where event-driven architecture and messaging services become useful.

In this article, I'll explore three AWS services that help applications communicate and process work more efficiently:

  • Amazon SQS — queues messages for processing.
  • Amazon SNS — distributes messages to multiple subscribers.
  • Amazon EventBridge — routes events to targets based on rules.

1. Why Do Applications Need Background Processing?

Consider a simple application where every operation happens inside one request.

Customer places an order
          |
          v
      Save order
          |
          v
   Update inventory
          |
          v
   Send confirmation
          |
          v
   Generate invoice
          |
          v
   Return response

If each operation runs sequentially, the customer may need to wait for all of them. If an external email service is slow, the entire request could take longer.

It also creates tight coupling: a problem in one dependency can affect the main request.

Instead, we can separate the immediate operation from background work.

Customer places an order
          |
          v
       Save order
          |
          v
   Queue background work
          |
          v
  Return response to customer
          |
          v
   Process tasks separately

Now the application can respond after completing the necessary synchronous work, while other operations happen independently.

This is one of the main ideas behind asynchronous processing.

2. Amazon SQS — Let Messages Wait in a Queue

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a managed message queuing service.

Think of it as a waiting line for tasks. A producer sends a message to the queue, and a consumer retrieves and processes it.

For example:

Order API
    |
    v
Amazon SQS Queue
    |
    v
Order Processing Worker
    |
    v
Update Inventory

The API doesn't need to wait for the worker to finish processing the message.

Why is SQS useful?

  • It helps decouple application components.
  • Messages can wait until consumers are ready to process them.
  • It helps absorb temporary traffic spikes.
  • Failed messages can be retried.
  • Dead-letter queues can isolate messages that repeatedly fail.

SQS offers Standard queues and FIFO queues. Standard queues provide high throughput with at-least-once delivery, so consumers should be designed to handle duplicate messages. FIFO queues support ordering within message groups and deduplication features, with their own throughput and configuration considerations.

One important concept is the visibility timeout. When a consumer receives a message, the message becomes temporarily invisible to other consumers. If processing succeeds, the consumer deletes it. If the message isn't deleted before the visibility timeout expires, it can become available again.

That is why reliable message processing needs error handling and idempotency.

3. Amazon SNS — Send One Message to Multiple Subscribers

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) is a managed publish/subscribe messaging service.

Instead of placing work in a queue for one consumer pattern, SNS can distribute a published message to multiple subscribers.

Imagine an order has been placed. Several systems need to react:

  • A notification service sends a confirmation.
  • An analytics service records the event.
  • Another service starts a fulfilment workflow.

SNS can help distribute the notification to these subscribers.

              Order Service
                    |
                    v
                 Amazon SNS
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |         |         |
          v         v         v
        SQS A     Lambda    Email
      Queue       Function  Endpoint

SNS supports different subscription types, including SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/S endpoints, and email, depending on the configuration and use case.

Why is SNS useful?

SNS is a good fit when multiple subscribers need to receive a notification about the same event.

For example, an order service can publish an OrderPlaced notification without needing to know the internal implementation of every subscriber.

That reduces direct dependencies between services.

A key distinction: SNS distributes messages; it is not a general-purpose durable work queue in the same way SQS is. Combining SNS with SQS can be useful when multiple consumers need their own queues and independent processing.

4. Amazon EventBridge — Route Events Based on Rules

Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus service that routes events to targets using rules.

An event describes something that happened, such as:

  • An order being placed.
  • A payment succeeding.
  • A file being uploaded to Amazon S3.
  • A scheduled task reaching its execution time.

EventBridge can inspect an event and route it to the targets whose rules match.

For example:

       OrderPlaced Event
               |
               v
       Amazon EventBridge
               |
        +------+------+
        |             |
        v             v
   Order Processor  Analytics
       Lambda        Target

You can define rules that match event attributes and send matching events to supported targets.

EventBridge is particularly useful for reacting to events from AWS services, your own applications, and supported SaaS integrations.

It also supports scheduled and time-based event patterns through its scheduling capabilities.

When should you use EventBridge?

Use it when you want to route events based on what happened, without tightly connecting the event producer to every downstream service.

For example, an application could react differently to OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, and OrderCancelled events.

5. SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge

These services can work together, but they solve different problems.

Feature Amazon SQS Amazon SNS Amazon EventBridge
Main purpose Queue messages for processing Distribute messages to subscribers Route events using rules
Core pattern Queue and consumer Publish/subscribe Event bus and targets
Typical use Background jobs Notifications to multiple subscribers Reacting to application or AWS events
Message handling Consumers poll or use supported integrations Pushes notifications to subscribers Routes matching events to targets
Useful feature Visibility timeout and dead-letter queues Multiple subscribers and filtering Event pattern matching and routing

Here's the simple mental model I use:

  • SQS: "Process this work when you're ready."
  • SNS: "Send this notification to these subscribers."
  • EventBridge: "When this event happens, route it to the appropriate target."

6. How They Work Together in a Real Application

Let's return to our online store.

After a customer places an order, the API saves the order and publishes an event. Different services can then handle different responsibilities.

An e-commerce application can use queues for background processing, notifications for multiple subscribers, and event rules to route events.

Here is a simplified architecture diagram in text form:

React Frontend
      |
      v
API Gateway
      |
      v
AWS Lambda
      |
      v
Save Order in DynamoDB
      |
      v
Publish OrderPlaced Event
      |
      v
Amazon EventBridge
      |
      +-------------------+
      |                   |
      v                   v
Order Processing       Analytics
      |
      v
Amazon SQS
      |
      v
Background Worker
      |
      v
Update Inventory / Fulfil Order

A separate notification workflow could use SNS to distribute an order notification to multiple subscribers.

The exact architecture depends on the requirements. For example, an SQS queue can be an EventBridge target, allowing the event to be routed to a durable queue for later processing.

This architecture separates the order API from slower background tasks. It also lets different components scale and fail independently to a degree, provided that retries, error handling, and downstream dependencies are designed correctly.

What happens when the order is placed?

  1. The React frontend sends a request to API Gateway.
  2. Lambda validates the request and saves the order in DynamoDB.
  3. The application publishes an order event.
  4. EventBridge evaluates its rules and routes matching events to configured targets.
  5. Background processing runs independently, potentially through SQS and a worker.
  6. SNS can distribute notifications to subscribers when needed.

One important production consideration: don't assume that saving an order and publishing an event are automatically one atomic operation. If the database write succeeds but event publishing fails, the system may need a reliable publishing strategy, such as the transactional outbox pattern, to avoid losing important events.

7. Reliability: Retries, Dead-Letter Queues, and Duplicate Messages

Asynchronous systems are powerful, but they introduce their own challenges.

What happens if a worker crashes while processing a message? What if a message is delivered more than once?

These are normal distributed-system problems.

Retries

Temporary failures may be resolved by retrying the operation. However, retries should be configured carefully to avoid overwhelming a failing dependency.

Dead-letter queues

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) can hold messages that exceed the configured retry or receive-count threshold. This gives you a way to investigate and recover messages that repeatedly fail.

Idempotency

An operation is idempotent when repeating it produces the same intended result rather than performing the effect multiple times.

For example, if a worker receives the same order-processing message twice, it should not deduct inventory twice unintentionally.

SQS Standard queues can deliver duplicate messages, and other event-driven workflows can also retry delivery. Design consumers with this possibility in mind.

Monitoring

CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms can help identify growing queue backlogs, processing failures, throttling, and other problems.

The goal isn't to assume messages will never fail. It's to design the application so failures can be detected and handled safely.

8. When Should You Use Each Service?

Choose the service based on the communication problem you're trying to solve.

Use Amazon SQS when:

  • Work needs to wait until a consumer is ready.
  • You want to separate request handling from background processing.
  • You need to buffer traffic spikes.
  • Consumers need to retry processing failed messages.

Use Amazon SNS when:

  • One message needs to reach multiple subscribers.
  • You want a publish/subscribe communication pattern.
  • Multiple systems need to react to the same notification.

Use Amazon EventBridge when:

  • Events need to be routed based on their content.
  • AWS services or applications generate events.
  • Different event types need different processing workflows.
  • You want event-driven integration without hardcoding every destination into the producer.

These are common patterns, not strict boundaries. Real architectures often combine these services.

9. My Main Takeaways

As I continue learning AWS, I'm realizing that building a reliable application involves more than deploying a backend and connecting a database.

It also means understanding how different components communicate, how failures are handled, and how background work can be processed without slowing down the user experience.

Here is the mental model I use:

  • Amazon SQS queues work for consumers.
  • Amazon SNS distributes messages to subscribers.
  • Amazon EventBridge routes events using rules.
  • AWS Lambda can execute event-driven processing.
  • Amazon DynamoDB can store application data.
  • Amazon CloudWatch helps monitor and troubleshoot the system.

The key lesson is that these services solve different communication problems. Choosing the right one depends on whether you need a queue, a notification mechanism, or event-based routing.

And in production, retries, duplicate handling, permissions, monitoring, and cost still matter.

I'm documenting my AWS learning journey one concept at a time. If you're learning cloud computing too, I'd love to hear what you're building and which AWS services you're exploring.

title: Can You Build a Backend Without Managing Servers? Understanding Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda & DynamoDB
summary:
When I first started learning AWS, I thought deploying a backend meant creating an EC2 instance, installing Node.js, configuring a web server, and keeping everything running.

That approach works. But what if you could build an API without managing the underlying servers yourself?

That is where serverless architecture comes in.

In this article, I’ll explore three AWS services that work well together to build serverless backends:

  • Amazon API Gateway — receives and manages API requests.
  • AWS Lambda — executes backend code.
  • Amazon DynamoDB — stores and retrieves data.

We’ll also look at how these services connect, explore a small Node.js example, and discuss when serverless makes sense in a real application.

1. What Does Serverless Actually Mean?

Serverless does not mean there are no servers.

Servers still exist. The difference is that AWS manages much of the underlying infrastructure, including server provisioning and infrastructure availability for these services.

Instead of managing a server yourself, you focus more on writing application code and defining how the services should work together.

For example, imagine you are building a task management application.

Users should be able to:

  • Create a task.
  • View their tasks.
  • Update a task.
  • Delete a task.

With a traditional backend, you might deploy a Node.js application on EC2 or ECS.

With a serverless approach, you could use API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB.

The basic flow looks like this:

User / React Frontend
         |
         v
   API Gateway
         |
         v
      Lambda
         |
         v
    DynamoDB
         |
         v
    JSON Response

Each service has a specific responsibility. This separation makes the architecture easier to understand and lets you scale different parts of the application according to their needs.

2. Amazon API Gateway — The Entry Point for Your API

Imagine your React frontend needs to request a list of tasks from your backend.

It might send a request such as:

GET /tasks

But where should that request go?

Amazon API Gateway provides an API entry point that clients can call. It can route requests to backend services such as Lambda functions.

It also supports capabilities such as authorization, request validation, throttling, and monitoring integrations, depending on the API type and configuration.

For example, you might define these routes:

HTTP Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /tasks Retrieve tasks
GET /tasks/{id} Retrieve one task
POST /tasks Create a task
PUT /tasks/{id} Update a task
DELETE /tasks/{id} Delete a task

Each route can be connected to a suitable Lambda function.

For example:

GET /tasks
    |
    v
getTasks Lambda

POST /tasks
    |
    v
createTask Lambda

API Gateway can also help protect an API from excessive requests through throttling and integrate with supported authorization mechanisms.

One important point: API Gateway is not your database, and it does not automatically make every API secure. Authentication, authorization, validation, and appropriate access policies still need to be configured.

  2. Read the task details.
  3. Validate the input.
  4. Store the task in DynamoDB.

You don't manually create more EC2 instances just to handle every increase in traffic.

Our backend now has an entry point and a way to execute code. But where should the application store its data?

For this example, we'll use Amazon DynamoDB.

DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database service that supports key-value and document data models.

Unlike a traditional relational database, DynamoDB does not require you to design every relationship around SQL tables and joins. Instead, you design tables and indexes around the access patterns your application needs.

Imagine storing tasks with fields such as:

{
  "userId": "user-123",
  "taskId": "task-001",
  "title": "Learn AWS Lambda",
  "completed": false
}

  • userId as the partition key.
  • taskId as the sort key.

Why choose DynamoDB?

Some useful characteristics include:

  • Managed infrastructure.
  • Flexible scaling options.
  • Low-latency access for suitable key-based access patterns.
  • Integration with Lambda and other AWS services.
  • On-demand capacity options for workloads where usage is difficult to predict.

But DynamoDB is not automatically the best database for every application.

If your application relies heavily on relational joins, complex SQL queries, or relational constraints, Amazon RDS or Amazon Aurora may be more suitable.

  2. The frontend sends a POST /tasks request.
  3. API Gateway receives the request and invokes the configured Lambda function.
  4. Lambda validates the input and executes the business logic.
  5. Lambda writes the task to DynamoDB using the AWS SDK.
  6. Lambda returns a response.
  7. API Gateway sends the response to the frontend.
  8. React updates the interface to show the result.

This architecture separates the frontend, API entry point, application logic, and database responsibilities.

Let's make the example a little more realistic.

Suppose we have a DynamoDB table named Tasks with userId as its partition key and taskId as its sort key.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import {
  DynamoDBDocumentClient,
  PutCommand,
} from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";

const client = new DynamoDBClient({});
const dynamoDB = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(client);

const TABLE_NAME = process.env.TABLE_NAME;

export const handler = async (event) => {
  try {
    if (!TABLE_NAME) {
      throw new Error("TABLE_NAME is not configured");
    }

    const { userId, title } = body;

      !title.trim()

      createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    };

        Item: task,
        ConditionExpression:

    );

      headers: {

      },

  • Sort key: taskId (String).

Frontend

   v
API Gateway
   |

   |

   |
   v

One reason serverless architecture is attractive is that it can reduce the amount of infrastructure management required as demand changes.

However, each component has its own limits and scaling behavior.

API Gateway

API Gateway can handle API traffic and supports configurable throttling and quotas. Your API may still receive throttling responses if configured limits or service quotas are exceeded.

Lambda

Lambda can increase concurrent executions as demand grows, within applicable concurrency quotas and account limits.

But more concurrent Lambda executions can also increase pressure on downstream services. If a function triggers expensive database operations, scaling the function alone will not solve the underlying bottleneck.

DynamoDB

Your key design and indexes also matter. A poorly designed access pattern can create hot partitions or inefficient queries even when the database itself is managed.

A cold start can occur when Lambda needs to initialize a new execution environment before processing a request. This may add latency.

The effect depends on factors such as runtime, initialization work, dependencies, memory configuration, and the execution environment.

For many applications, occasional cold starts are acceptable. For latency-sensitive workloads, measure actual performance and evaluate options such as reducing initialization work or using provisioned concurrency where appropriate.

Serverless makes infrastructure management easier in many cases, but it doesn't remove the need for performance testing.

This is an important lesson: serverless is a deployment model, not a guarantee of lower cost.

With Lambda, costs can depend on request volume, execution duration, configured memory, and other applicable charges.

For a small application with occasional requests, a serverless design can be cost-effective because you don't need to maintain an always-running application server for every request.

Feature AWS Lambda EC2 ECS with Fargate

Application model Event-driven functions Applications or services on virtual machines Containerized applications
Scaling Based on invocations and concurrency settings Configure scaling for instances and workloads Configure service/task scaling
Long-running processes Subject to function execution limits Suitable Suitable, subject to task and service configuration
Runtime control Supported Lambda runtimes and execution model High control Container-level control
Operational effort Often lower for suitable workloads Often higher Moderate, depending on the application
Good fit APIs, event handlers, scheduled tasks Custom server environments and broad workloads Containerized APIs, workers, and services

Lambda is especially useful when work can be broken into event-driven executions.

EC2 is useful when you need control over the virtual machine and its environment.

ECS with Fargate is useful when you want to run containers without managing the underlying EC2 instances yourself.

These services are not mutually exclusive. A real application can use Lambda for event-driven operations and ECS/Fargate for a long-running API or worker.

Choose based on the workload, operational requirements, performance expectations, and cost—not just which service sounds newer.

11. What I Would Consider Before Deploying to Production

Before deploying a serverless API for real users, I would check the following:

  • [ ] Configure API routes and appropriate authorization.
  • [ ] Validate request bodies and query parameters.
  • [ ] Derive user identity from verified authentication rather than trusting client-supplied identity fields.
  • [ ] Use a least-privilege Lambda execution role.
  • [ ] Design DynamoDB keys and indexes around real access patterns.
  • [ ] Configure environment variables and manage any required secrets safely.
  • [ ] Add useful logs, metrics, alarms, and tracing where appropriate.
  • [ ] Handle errors and retries carefully.
  • [ ] Make operations safe to retry where duplicate processing is possible.
  • [ ] Set suitable timeouts, concurrency limits, and throttling.
  • [ ] Test under realistic traffic and estimate costs.
  • [ ] Deploy through a repeatable infrastructure-as-code and CI/CD process.

One detail worth emphasizing is idempotency. Distributed systems can retry requests or events after failures. If a repeated operation would create duplicate records, charge a customer twice, or trigger the same action repeatedly, the application needs a strategy to prevent that.

For asynchronous workflows, services such as Amazon SQS can help decouple components. But queue-based processing also requires careful retry handling, dead-letter queues where appropriate, and idempotent consumers.

12. When Should You Use This Architecture?

A serverless API built with API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB is worth considering when:

  • You are building a small or medium-sized API.
  • Traffic is variable or difficult to predict.
  • You want to reduce server administration.
  • Your application fits DynamoDB's data model and access patterns.
  • You want to integrate backend operations with events from other AWS services.
  • You prefer managed services for the initial deployment.

It may be less suitable when:

  • Your application depends heavily on relational queries and complex joins.
  • You need sustained, long-running processing beyond Lambda's execution limits.
  • You require very predictable low latency and have not accounted for initialization behavior.
  • Your workload has steady high utilization and another compute model may offer better economics.
  • You need operating-system or runtime control that the chosen serverless service does not provide.

These are trade-offs, not absolute rules. The best architecture depends on the actual requirements.

13. My Main Takeaways

After learning about API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, I think the biggest benefit of serverless is the change in focus.

Instead of spending as much time managing servers, you can spend more time designing APIs, writing business logic, securing data access, and understanding how application components interact.

Here is the mental model I use:

  • API Gateway receives and routes API requests.
  • Lambda executes backend logic.
  • DynamoDB stores and retrieves data.
  • IAM controls AWS permissions.
  • Cognito or another identity provider can support authentication.
  • CloudWatch helps monitor and troubleshoot the system.
  • SQS can decouple asynchronous work when the application needs it.

But serverless does not mean architecture disappears. You still need to design for security, failures, retries, performance, and cost.

That is what makes learning AWS interesting: the goal isn't simply to learn what each service does. It's to understand how to combine the services to solve a real problem.

What's next?

I'm continuing my AWS learning journey by exploring how these services fit into real application architectures, from containerized backends to serverless APIs and automated deployments.

If you're also learning AWS, I'd love to hear what you're building and which services you're exploring.

This code is a handler example, not a complete deployment tutorial. You still need to create the table, configure the Lambda runtime and execution role, connect the function to API Gateway, and test the request and response formats.

7. What About Authentication and Security?

A serverless backend still needs security. AWS managing the infrastructure does not automatically secure your application's business logic or data.

Here are some services and controls that may be useful.

AWS IAM

IAM controls which AWS resources and actions an identity can access.

For this architecture, the Lambda execution role should grant only the permissions the function needs, such as writing to one DynamoDB table.

Amazon Cognito or another authentication provider

If users need to sign in, you need an authentication mechanism.

Amazon Cognito can provide user sign-up, sign-in, and token-based authentication capabilities. API Gateway can be configured to validate supported authorization tokens, depending on the API type and setup.

Authentication identifies the caller. Your application must still enforce authorization: a signed-in user should not automatically have access to every other user's tasks.

AWS Secrets Manager

If the application needs external API credentials or other secrets, Secrets Manager can store and manage them.

DynamoDB access through the Lambda execution role generally does not require a database password. Avoid adding unnecessary credentials simply because other backend architectures use them.

Amazon CloudWatch

CloudWatch can collect Lambda logs, metrics, and alarms. These help you investigate errors, monitor latency, and detect unusual invocation or throttling patterns.

A simple security model 

Frontend
   |
   v
API Gateway
   |
   +--> Validate authentication
   |
   v
Lambda Execution Role
   |
   +--> Only required DynamoDB actions
   |
   v
DynamoDB Table

The exact configuration depends on the application's requirements, but the core principle stays the same: grant only the permissions required, and verify who is allowed to access each user's data.

8. What Happens When Traffic Increases?

One reason serverless architecture is attractive is that it can reduce the amount of infrastructure management required as demand changes.

However, each component has its own limits and scaling behavior.

API Gateway

API Gateway can handle API traffic and supports configurable throttling and quotas. Your API may still receive throttling responses if configured limits or service quotas are exceeded.

Lambda

Lambda can increase concurrent executions as demand grows, within applicable concurrency quotas and account limits.

But more concurrent Lambda executions can also increase pressure on downstream services. If a function triggers expensive database operations, scaling the function alone will not solve the underlying bottleneck.

DynamoDB

DynamoDB offers on-demand and provisioned capacity modes. The appropriate choice depends on traffic patterns, predictability, and cost requirements.

Your key design and indexes also matter. A poorly designed access pattern can create hot partitions or inefficient queries even when the database itself is managed.

What about cold starts?

A cold start can occur when Lambda needs to initialize a new execution environment before processing a request. This may add latency.

The effect depends on factors such as runtime, initialization work, dependencies, memory configuration, and the execution environment.

For many applications, occasional cold starts are acceptable. For latency-sensitive workloads, measure actual performance and evaluate options such as reducing initialization work or using provisioned concurrency where appropriate.

Serverless makes infrastructure management easier in many cases, but it doesn't remove the need for performance testing.

9. Serverless Is Not Always Cheaper

This is an important lesson: serverless is a deployment model, not a guarantee of lower cost.

With Lambda, costs can depend on request volume, execution duration, configured memory, and other applicable charges.

API Gateway pricing depends on the API type and usage. DynamoDB costs depend on the capacity mode, requests, storage, and additional features.

For a small application with occasional requests, a serverless design can be cost-effective because you don't need to maintain an always-running application server for every request.

For a high-volume application with predictable, sustained workloads, another architecture might be more economical. You need to compare actual usage and current pricing rather than assume one model always wins.

Remember to consider supporting services, logging volume, data transfer, provisioned capacity, and other configuration choices when estimating costs.

10. Lambda vs EC2 vs ECS/Fargate

Since I've been learning EC2, Docker, Amazon ECR, ECS, and Fargate, I find it useful to compare these approaches.

Feature AWS Lambda EC2 ECS with Fargate
Infrastructure management AWS manages the execution infrastructure You manage the instances and operating system AWS manages the underlying compute infrastructure
Application model Event-driven functions Applications or services on virtual machines Containerized applications
Scaling Based on invocations and concurrency settings Configure scaling for instances and workloads Configure service/task scaling
Long-running processes Subject to function execution limits Suitable Suitable, subject to task and service configuration
Runtime control Supported Lambda runtimes and execution model High control Container-level control
Operational effort Often lower for suitable workloads Often higher Moderate, depending on the application
Good fit APIs, event handlers, scheduled tasks Custom server environments and broad workloads Containerized APIs, workers, and services

Lambda is especially useful when work can be broken into event-driven executions.

EC2 is useful when you need control over the virtual machine and its environment.

ECS with Fargate is useful when you want to run containers without managing the underlying EC2 instances yourself.

These services are not mutually exclusive. A real application can use Lambda for event-driven operations and ECS/Fargate for a long-running API or worker.

Choose based on the workload, operational requirements, performance expectations, and cost—not just which service sounds newer.

11. What I Would Consider Before Deploying to Production

Before deploying a serverless API for real users, I would check the following:

  • [ ] Configure API routes and appropriate authorization.
  • [ ] Validate request bodies and query parameters.
  • [ ] Derive user identity from verified authentication rather than trusting client-supplied identity fields.
  • [ ] Use a least-privilege Lambda execution role.
  • [ ] Design DynamoDB keys and indexes around real access patterns.
  • [ ] Configure environment variables and manage any required secrets safely.
  • [ ] Add useful logs, metrics, alarms, and tracing where appropriate.
  • [ ] Handle errors and retries carefully.
  • [ ] Make operations safe to retry where duplicate processing is possible.
  • [ ] Set suitable timeouts, concurrency limits, and throttling.
  • [ ] Test under realistic traffic and estimate costs.
  • [ ] Deploy through a repeatable infrastructure-as-code and CI/CD process.

One detail worth emphasizing is idempotency. Distributed systems can retry requests or events after failures. If a repeated operation would create duplicate records, charge a customer twice, or trigger the same action repeatedly, the application needs a strategy to prevent that.

For asynchronous workflows, services such as Amazon SQS can help decouple components. But queue-based processing also requires careful retry handling, dead-letter queues where appropriate, and idempotent consumers.

12. When Should You Use This Architecture?

A serverless API built with API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB is worth considering when:

  • You are building a small or medium-sized API.
  • Traffic is variable or difficult to predict.
  • You want to reduce server administration.
  • Your application fits DynamoDB's data model and access patterns.
  • You want to integrate backend operations with events from other AWS services.
  • You prefer managed services for the initial deployment.

It may be less suitable when:

  • Your application depends heavily on relational queries and complex joins.
  • You need sustained, long-running processing beyond Lambda's execution limits.
  • You require very predictable low latency and have not accounted for initialization behavior.
  • Your workload has steady high utilization and another compute model may offer better economics.
  • You need operating-system or runtime control that the chosen serverless service does not provide.

These are trade-offs, not absolute rules. The best architecture depends on the actual requirements.

13. My Main Takeaways

After learning about API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, I think the biggest benefit of serverless is the change in focus.

Instead of spending as much time managing servers, you can spend more time designing APIs, writing business logic, securing data access, and understanding how application components interact.

Here is the mental model I use:

  • API Gateway receives and routes API requests.
  • Lambda executes backend logic.
  • DynamoDB stores and retrieves data.
  • IAM controls AWS permissions.
  • Cognito or another identity provider can support authentication.
  • CloudWatch helps monitor and troubleshoot the system.
  • SQS can decouple asynchronous work when the application needs it.

But serverless does not mean architecture disappears. You still need to design for security, failures, retries, performance, and cost.

That is what makes learning AWS interesting: the goal isn't simply to learn what each service does. It's to understand how to combine the services to solve a real problem.

What's next?

I'm continuing my AWS learning journey by exploring how these services fit into real application architectures, from containerized backends to serverless APIs and automated deployments.

If you're also learning AWS, I'd love to hear what you're building and which services you're exploring.
