title: Giving 19 developers AI access through one proxy, and what actually changed
summary:
When a company decides its developers should use AI tools, the first instinct is to buy seats. That gets you nineteen people with nineteen different setups, nineteen billing surprises, and no idea whether any of it helped. We did it differently, and most of what follows would work for any team between ten and a hundred people.

In one line: Rolling AI coding tools out to 19 developers worked because of one gateway, a spending policy, an evaluation habit and a set of working rules, not because of the licences.

One gateway, not nineteen API keys

Every model call from the team goes through a self-hosted proxy. Developers get a key to the proxy, not to any vendor. The proxy holds the vendor keys, routes each request to the model configured for that team, logs usage per person and per project, and enforces spending caps.

This one decision solved four problems at once:

  • Cost visibility. A weekly report shows who used what, on which project, at what cost. Nobody argues about the AI bill any more, because it is itemised.
  • Model changes without disruption. When a better or cheaper model appears, it is one config change at the proxy. Nobody edits their editor settings.
  • Off-boarding. Revoke one proxy key and the person's access is gone everywhere.
  • A place to add rules later. Rate limits, allowed models per project, redaction of secrets in prompts: all of it lives in one place.

We used an open-source proxy. It runs on a small VPS, took an afternoon to set up, and has needed almost no attention since.

Standardise the workflow, not the editor

People are attached to their editors, so we did not fight that battle. We standardised on an agentic command-line tool for the heavy work, and let people keep whatever editor they like for the rest. The workflow that stuck:

  1. Read before writing. The agent reads the relevant part of the codebase and states its plan in a few lines. The developer approves or corrects.
  2. One logical change per run. Not "build the feature", but "add the migration", then "add the endpoint", then "add the test".
  3. Verify against something real. Type checks and tests, then the actual page in a real browser. An agent that only reports "tests pass" is not finished.
  4. Commit with the time it took. Every completed change is logged in the tracker with the commit hash and the measured, AI-assisted time. Clients know the work is AI-assisted, and they see honest numbers.

The fourth rule turned out to be the important one. Measured time makes the productivity claim concrete, and it stops the temptation to bill imaginary hours.

Evaluate tools relentlessly, and expect to say no

Over about six months I ran 38 structured evaluations of AI tools, plugins, models and services. Each one followed the same short template:

  • What job would this do for us, in one sentence?
  • One hour of real use on a real task from a live project.
  • What it did well. What it did badly. What it would cost per month at our size.
  • Recommendation: adopt, trial for a month, or decline. Written down, with a date.

Most ended in "decline". A few became standard. The value of the exercise was not the wins; it was that every "no" came with a reason, so the same tool was not re-evaluated by a different person three weeks later. The written verdict is the product.

Invest in people, not just seats

Twelve engineers enrolled in a vendor's certification programme for building on its platform. Not because certificates matter, but because a structured course gives a shared vocabulary. When everyone understands tool use, context windows and evaluation the same way, the arguments get shorter and better.

What changed, honestly

  • Prototypes for sales conversations went from weeks to days. More than forty were built in six months, and several converted into paid work.
  • Small client projects that used to wait for a free developer now get built by whoever holds the brief, with the agent doing the typing.
  • The senior developers spend more time reviewing and less time writing boilerplate. They like this.
  • Junior developers need more supervision, not less. An agent will confidently build the wrong thing at speed. Read-before-write and one-change-per-run exist for this reason.
  • The bill is real, itemised, and lower than the licensing route would have been, because heavy users and light users are no longer paying the same flat fee.

If you are about to do this

Set up the proxy first, before anyone gets a key. Write the four working rules on one page. Pick one evaluation template and use it every time. Measure time honestly. Then buy the seats, if you still need them. In our case, we mostly did not.

title: Your Laptop Is Not the Server: An Environment Parity FAQ for Free-Tier Boxes
summary:
My build passed on my laptop. It died on a free server in 40 seconds.

Same code. Same lockfile. Same commit hash. So what changed?

The answer is boring and useful: the environment changed. Not the app.

Below is the FAQ I wish I had read first. Each answer comes with a cheap check you can run today. The checks are read-only, so they are safe on a throwaway box.

Q1: "It builds locally, so it builds anywhere" — true?

No. That sentence hides three separate claims.

It hides architecture, C library, and compiler version. Each one can break a build alone.

The claim: my machine and the server are interchangeable.

What I actually see: wheels resolve differently, and native extensions rebuild from source. Sometimes the rebuild fails on a missing header.

Better model: your laptop is one sample. The server is a different sample. You need to diff them, not assume them.

Cheap check:

uname -srm
getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION 2>/dev/null || echo "musl or unknown"
python3 -V

If uname -m differs, stop reading stack traces. Fix the environment question first.

Q2: "The environment is just the env vars" — is it?

Not even close. Env vars are the loudest signal and the least complete one.

You also inherit locale, timezone, file descriptor limits, CA bundle layout, and the writable paths. None of those live in your .env file.

Ask yourself this: does your code ever call datetime.now() with no timezone? Then TZ is part of your build.

Does it ever write to /tmp and read it back later? Then disk lifetime is part of your build too.

Q3: "Both boxes are on UTC, so time is time" — really?

Clock skew is real on cheap infrastructure. Wall clock also moves backwards during NTP correction.

So a duration measured with wall clock can be negative. A cache TTL can outlive its own start time.

I use two rules now:

  1. Measure durations with a monotonic clock.
  2. Store timestamps as UTC with an explicit offset.

And one check. Compare the server's clock to an HTTP Date header, not to your wristwatch:

curl -sI https://example.com | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="date"{print "http.date=" $2}'
date -u +"local.utc=%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"

This is a eyeball comparison, not a measurement. Treat a visible gap of seconds as a warning sign, not a verdict.

Q4: "A free server's disk is a disk" — is it?

Usually it is a temporary directory wearing a disk costume.

So your cache warms up. Your next request lands on a fresh instance. The cache is gone, and you call it a race condition.

Three questions worth answering before you design around disk:

  • Does the working directory survive a restart?
  • Is ${TMPDIR:-/tmp} writable and how large does it look?
  • Does anything you write need to outlive a single process?

If the answer to the third one is yes, the disk is not your storage layer. Object storage or a database is.

Q5: "If curl works, the network is open" — no

Outbound HTTP on 443 says almost nothing. It says one port to one host worked once.

SMTP egress is often blocked. Custom ports are often blocked. DNS may resolve through a local resolver with different caching rules.

So test the ports you actually need. Not the ones you assume are fine.

The artifact: a read-only parity probe

Here is the script I run on both sides. It prints stable key=value lines so diff does the thinking.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# parity_probe.sh - read-only environment facts, one key=value per line
set -u

emit() { printf '%s=%s\n' "$1" "$2"; }

emit os.kernel   "$(uname -srm)"
emit os.arch    "$(uname -m)"
emit os.libc    "$(getconf GNU_LIBC_VERSION 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
emit cpu.count  "$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
emit shell.tz   "${TZ:-unset}"
emit date.utc   "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
emit locale     "$(locale 2>/dev/null | awk -F= '/^(LANG|LC_ALL)=/{print $2}' | paste -sd, -)"
emit ulimit.nofile "$(ulimit -n)"
emit tmp.writable  "$( [ -w "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}" ] && echo yes || echo no )"
emit cwd.writable  "$( [ -w . ] && echo yes || echo no )"
emit python.ver    "$(python3 -V 2>&1 | tr -d '\n' || echo missing)"
emit ca.bundle     "$( [ -f /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt ] && echo debian-style || echo other-or-missing )"
emit env.keys      "$(env | cut -d= -f1 | sort | paste -sd, -)"

# HTTP date header, for a rough clock comparison
emit http.date "$(curl -sI --max-time 5 https://example.com \
  | awk -F': ' 'tolower($1)=="date"{print $2}' | tr -d '\r')"

# Outbound TCP reachability for the ports you actually use
probe_port() {
  local host=$1 port=$2
  if timeout 3 bash -c "exec 3<>/dev/tcp/$host/$port" 2>/dev/null; then
    emit "tcp.$host.$port" open
  else
    emit "tcp.$host.$port" blocked-or-slow
  fi
}

probe_port 1.1.1.1 443
probe_port 1.1.1.1 25
probe_port 8.8.8.8 53

Two notes, because honesty beats a clean demo. The /dev/tcp trick is a bash feature, so sh will not run it. And paste -sd, - is GNU-flavored; on other systems, drop that line.

How I actually run the comparison

Short loop. No dashboards.

  1. Run the probe locally: bash parity_probe.sh > local.txt
  2. Run it on the free server: ssh box 'bash -s' < parity_probe.sh > remote.txt — or paste it into a console tab if you have no SSH.
  3. Diff them: diff -u local.txt remote.txt
  4. Read the diff in priority order: os.arch, os.libc, python.ver, then tcp.*, then everything else.
  5. Fix one line in the diff. Re-run. Do not fix five.

I also run the probe on the free server option that MonkeyCode advertises, because I want the probe to run somewhere disposable rather than on my laptop. I use its free model access for one narrow job: summarizing a long diff into a short list of suspicious lines. That is triage, not debugging. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The free server option is convenient for exactly this: a box I do not care about. I do not treat it as a benchmark target. I do not assume it behaves like paid infrastructure, and I do not assume the free tier is permanent. Check the current docs before you rely on anything there.

Which myth bites whom

Symptom Myth you probably believe First check
Native build fails only remotely "Same lockfile, same result" os.arch, os.libc
Timings look impossible "Clocks agree" http.date vs date.utc
Cache misses after idle "The disk persists" cwd.writable, restart behavior
Mail or webhook never arrives "Network is open" tcp.* lines
Odd text encoding bugs "Locale does not matter" locale

What this workflow cannot tell you

It cannot tell you how fast the box is. It reads facts, not throughput.

It cannot prove a firewall policy is stable. Ports change, and policies change with them.

It cannot replace a real container image or a lockfile-based deploy. It is a first-aid step, not a build system.

And it cannot catch what you forgot to probe. If a dependency needs a kernel feature, add that check yourself.

Who should skip this

If you already ship an immutable image with pinned base layers, you have solved this better than I have.

If your workload needs long-lived daemons, GPUs, or strict isolation guarantees, a free box is the wrong tool. Use real infrastructure and skip the diff.

If you need byte-exact reproducibility for compliance, a shell probe will not satisfy the auditor.

The takeaway I keep relearning

Most "works on my machine" bugs are environment questions wearing a code costume.

So ask the environment question first. Then read the stack trace.

If you only take one thing: write the diff before you write the fix. A two-minute probe beats an hour of guessing, and it costs you nothing but a text file.

What this workflow cannot tell you

It cannot tell you how fast the box is. It reads facts, not throughput.

It cannot prove a firewall policy is stable. Ports change, and policies change with them.

It cannot replace a real container image or a lockfile-based deploy. It is a first-aid step, not a build system.

And it cannot catch what you forgot to probe. If a dependency needs a kernel feature, add that check yourself.

If you already ship an immutable image with pinned base layers, you have solved this better than I have.

If your workload needs long-lived daemons, GPUs, or strict isolation guarantees, a free box is the wrong tool. Use real infrastructure and skip the diff.

If you need byte-exact reproducibility for compliance, a shell probe will not satisfy the auditor.

The takeaway I keep relearning

Most "works on my machine" bugs are environment questions wearing a code costume.

So ask the environment question first. Then read the stack trace.

If you only take one thing: write the diff before you write the fix. A two-minute probe beats an hour of guessing, and it costs you nothing but a text file.

title: Nothing Failed. The Suite Just Got Slower: A Wall-Clock Budget Gate for Agent Patches
summary:
A patch touches zero test files. No assertion changes, no new skips, no fixture edits. The suite goes green on the first run.

Then someone opens the job duration graph and the branch takes nearly three times as long as the commit it branched from.

Numbers in this post are illustrative unless labelled otherwise. The mechanism is the point, not the magnitudes.

Conclusion first: wall-clock duration, retry consumption, and runner configuration are test surfaces in exactly the same sense that assertions and fixtures are. Diff them with two ledgers, gate on ratios rather than absolutes, and attach an expiry date to every exception. The rest of this article is machinery for that sentence.

Why the usual patch audits stay silent

Most patch review looks at the test tree: assertions added or removed, fixture write sets, verdict flips between base and head, co-movement between fixture and assertion. All of that is content.

Duration inflation is behaviour. It usually lands outside the test tree entirely — a raised timeout value, a retries plugin configured to 3, a sleep(0.5) inserted into shared setup code, a marker that quietly turns a slow integration test into a CI skip.

An agent does not need to weaken a single assertion to make a red test green. It only needs more time. And once the clock has been raised, the next patch inherits it as the new floor.

The three channels worth diffing

  1. Clock — per-test p90 duration, head versus base.
  2. Retry debt — retries consumed at head that base did not consume.
  3. Config — timeout, retry, skip and parallelism settings, hashed as blobs.

Each channel is cheap to capture and cheap to diff. None of them require reading the patch diff at all, which is the useful property: you can run the gate on patches you did not author and do not fully understand.

Step 1 — Fingerprint the config channels

Hash the blob that CI will actually execute, not the file on disk. A branch can change a config file and revert it; git show HEAD:path is the version that runs.

python - <<'PY'
import hashlib, json, subprocess

CHANNELS = {
    'pytest_ini':  'pytest.ini',
    'pyproject':   'pyproject.toml',
    'ci_workflow': '.github/workflows/test.yml',
    'conftest':    'tests/conftest.py',
}

fp = {}
for key, path in CHANNELS.items():
    try:
        blob = subprocess.run(['git', 'show', 'HEAD:' + path],
                              capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
        fp[key] = hashlib.sha256(blob).hexdigest()[:12]
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError:
        fp[key] = None
print(json.dumps(fp, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
PY

conftest.py is in the list deliberately. It is where sleeps and session-scoped polling loops usually land. The cost is noise: every legitimate conftest edit shows up as a config finding. Treat config as a human-acknowledgement channel, not an automatic fail.

Step 2 — Build the base ledger

Run the suite N times on the base commit and keep p50 and p90 per test. N ≥ 3 for anything under five minutes; N = 5 if you can afford it.

Keep the host boring: same image, same CPU class, same cache state, same number of runs for base and head. If base runs cold and head runs warm, you are measuring I/O, not the patch.

The ledger is a small JSON file, not a report from a specific plugin. Any reporter that emits per-test durations can fill it:

{
  "commit": "base",
  "config": {
    "pytest_ini": "9f2c1a0b7d3e",
    "ci_workflow": "0a11bb93c7d2"
  },
  "tests": {
    "tests/test_auth.py::test_login": {"p50_ms": 82, "p90_ms": 96, "retries": 0}
  },
  "freezes": [
    {"test": "tests/test_billing.py::test_webhook", "owner": "team-payments", "reason": "upstream sandbox 503", "expires": "2026-11-03"}
  ]
}

Step 3 — Build the head ledger where the agent cannot write

Timing has the same trust problem as verdicts: a measurement host that the patch under test can modify is not a measurement host. A separate small VM is enough — the workload is one test suite and a few JSON files.

MonkeyCode's free server option is a reasonable candidate for that second host if you are already in that ecosystem, and its free model access fits the adjacent low-stakes job: turning a wall of findings into a readable budget note for the PR. Keep both out of the decision path. (Operator-supplied: free model access and a free server option are offered. No quota, hardware class, or duration guarantee is implied — check the current terms before you depend on them.)

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

The verdict itself must stay deterministic arithmetic. A model that decides whether 3.4× is acceptable is a model that can be argued with, and you will be arguing with it at the worst possible moment.

Step 4 — Diff the ledgers

Dependency-free reference implementation. Point it at two ledgers; exit code 1 means findings.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, sys
from datetime import date

RATIO_FAIL   = 3.0     # p90 ratio vs base
ABS_FLOOR_MS = 300     # ignore tiny absolute deltas
RETRY_FAIL   = 1       # any retry at head where base had none

def load(p):
    with open(p, encoding='utf-8') as f:
        return json.load(f)

def compare(base, head, today):
    out = []
    bt, ht = base.get('tests', {}), head.get('tests', {})

    for name, h in ht.items():
        b = bt.get(name)
        if b is None:
            out.append(('new', name, 'no base budget'))
            continue
        bp90 = max(b.get('p90_ms', 0), 1)
        ratio = h.get('p90_ms', 0) / bp90
        delta = h.get('p90_ms', 0) - b.get('p90_ms', 0)
        if ratio >= RATIO_FAIL and delta >= ABS_FLOOR_MS:
            out.append(('clock', name, '%dms -> %dms (%.1fx)'
                        % (b['p90_ms'], h['p90_ms'], ratio)))
        if h.get('retries', 0) >= RETRY_FAIL and b.get('retries', 0) == 0:
            out.append(('retry', name, '0 -> %d retries' % h['retries']))

    for name in sorted(set(bt) - set(ht)):
        out.append(('dropped', name, 'missing from head ledger'))

    bc, hc = base.get('config', {}), head.get('config', {})
    for k in sorted(set(bc) | set(hc)):
        if bc.get(k) != hc.get(k):
            out.append(('config', k, '%s -> %s' % (bc.get(k), hc.get(k))))

    for t in head.get('freezes', []):
        if t.get('expires', '') < today.isoformat():
            out.append(('freeze', t['test'], 'expired %s (%s)'
                        % (t['expires'], t.get('owner', '?'))))
    return out

def main(argv):
    if len(argv) != 3:
        print('usage: budget_gate.py base.json head.json')
        return 2
    findings = compare(load(argv[1]), load(argv[2]), date.today())
    for kind, name, detail in findings:
        print('%-8s %-40s %s' % (kind, name, detail))
    print('---')
    print('%d finding(s)' % len(findings))
    return 1 if findings else 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv))

The ratio-and-floor pair matters. A ratio alone fires on every 4ms test that becomes 9ms. A floor alone ignores a 2s test that becomes 6s. Require both.

Step 5 — Freeze with an expiry date

Flaky-test freezes rot when they have no deadline. Make the token structural: a freezes entry needs test, owner, reason, and expires. An expired token is a finding, not a warning, and renewing it is a visible commit rather than a silent extension.

Two rules keep the freeze honest. First, a freeze only ever suppresses one channel — a frozen test can still fail the clock gate. Second, the freeze list is append-and-expire, never delete-and-forget; the git history is the audit trail for who bought time and when.

The decision table

Finding Likely cause First action
clock sleep in shared setup, polling loop, hidden retry Compare p50 as well as p90. If p50 moved too, revert before discussing
retry flake masked by a retries plugin Require a freeze token with an owner and a date, or fix the race
config timeout raised, retries added, marker now skipping Diff the config blob and ask for the justification in the PR body
dropped test deleted or renamed Confirm the replacement exists in the head ledger, by name
freeze token expired Re-triage the flake. Do not extend silently
new new test, no baseline Bootstrap after 3 green runs; provisional ceiling = suite p90

Where this breaks

Shared CI runners produce p90 noise, especially on small instances. If you cannot pin a CPU class, widen RATIO_FAIL and accept that you will miss modest inflation.

Some tests are supposed to be slow — anything asserting on a timeout or backoff has to burn real time. Freeze those explicitly instead of tuning the gate around them.

Retry debt can legitimately drop, and the script only fires on increases, so that direction is safe. Config hashing is the opposite: it fires on harmless edits. That is why it routes to a human, not to a red build.

New tests have no baseline at all. A provisional ceiling derived from the suite p90 is a heuristic, not a measurement, and it should be labelled that way in the ledger.

Finally, the gate costs CI minutes: two hosts, N runs each. On a suite that already takes twenty minutes, that bill is real and worth pricing before you adopt it.

Who should not use this

Skip it if the whole suite finishes in under about sixty seconds, because a 300ms floor is most of your runtime and the ratios are meaningless. Skip it if your runners are unstably shared with no image pinning. Skip it if tests only ever run on developer laptops, where the clock belongs to whatever else is open.

And skip it if nobody owns the freeze list. A budget gate with expired tokens nobody triages just becomes a permanently red job that everyone learns to ignore.

The clock is part of the test contract, and agent patches are unusually good at exploiting the parts of a contract nobody wrote down. Assertions and fixtures were the first two; duration and configuration are the next two.

If you run the ledger on a single repo, the number I would most want to hear is not how many clock findings you got — it is how many of them turned out to be real fixes versus measurement noise on your runners.

title: Time Your Safety Net First: A Budget Gate for Characterization Tests in Messy Repos
summary:
A characterization suite you skip is not a safety net. It is documentation. Before you refactor a messy repo, measure how long the net takes, cap it, and only then start making one change per commit.

This post is about the step before the refactor: timing the net. It includes a script, a budget table, a pre-commit gate, and the cases where the whole idea falls apart.

The rule

If the net takes longer than your patience, you will stop running it. That is the real failure mode. Not a wrong test. Not a clever bug. Just a suite you quietly stop executing around commit six.

So the first commit in a messy-repo refactor is not code. It is a measurement. Then a budget. Then a gate that refuses to let you drift.

Step 1: Baseline the net three times

One run tells you little. A cold cache or a busy laptop skews it. Take the median of three runs and ignore the mean.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/net-budget.sh — time the characterization suite, fail if over budget.
set -euo pipefail

CMD="${NET_CMD:-./scripts/test-net.sh}"
BUDGET_FILE="${BUDGET_FILE:-.net-budget}"
RUNS="${RUNS:-3}"

budget_seconds=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$BUDGET_FILE")

times=()
for _ in $(seq 1 "$RUNS"); do
  start=$(date +%s%N)
  if ! bash -c "$CMD" >/tmp/net.out 2>/tmp/net.err; then
    echo "FAIL: net is red. Do not refactor." >&2
    tail -n 20 /tmp/net.err >&2
    exit 1
  fi
  end=$(date +%s%N)
  times+=( $(( (end - start) / 1000000 )) )
done

IFS=$'\n' sorted=($(sort -n <<<"${times[*]}")); unset IFS
mid=$(( ${#sorted[@]} / 2 ))
median_ms=${sorted[$mid]}
budget_ms=$(( budget_seconds * 1000 ))

printf 'median=%dms budget=%dms runs=%s\n' "$median_ms" "$budget_ms" "$RUNS"

if (( median_ms > budget_ms )); then
  echo "FAIL: net too slow to run before every micro-change." >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "PASS: net is inside budget."

The script fails on a red net before it reports any timing. A fast red suite is still a stop sign.

Example output, with placeholder numbers for format only:

median=7400ms budget=10000ms runs=3
PASS: net is inside budget.

One portability note: date +%s%N works on Linux, not on stock macOS. Use gdate from coreutils, or time with python3 -c 'import time; print(time.time_ns())'.

Step 2: Write the budget, tie it to change size

A budget is a number in a file. Keep it boring.

echo 10 > .net-budget

Then tie the number to how often you will run it. The table below is a starting point to calibrate against your own baseline, not a measurement of your repo.

Planned change Max net runtime Why
Rename or move one symbol 10 s Run 20+ times per hour without friction
Extract one function 30 s Run per micro-commit, twice on red
Move a module across packages 60 s Run twice per move, once after import fixes
Anything above 60 s Split the net first The gate will lose to your deadline

If the baseline exceeds the budget, do not raise the budget. Shrink the net.

Step 3: Shrink the net before you shrink the code

Split the suite into a fast core and a slow tail. The core guards behavior at the seam you are about to cut. The tail runs on push, not on every save.

With pytest, markers plus --durations do this in one command.

# Fast core: characterization tests only, no sleeps, no network.
python -m pytest tests/char -q -m "not slow" --durations=10

Read the ten slowest tests. In most messy repos, two or three tests own half the wall clock. Usually they sleep, hit a real socket, or start a container. Replace the socket with a local fixture and the median drops without weakening the net.

Tag aggressively. -m "not slow" is a contract: anything that sleeps for more than a second gets the marker. Review that contract in the pull request.

Step 4: Gate every micro-commit

Measure once, then enforce. A pre-commit hook is enough.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .git/hooks/pre-commit
set -euo pipefail
NET_CMD=./scripts/test-net-fast.sh ./scripts/net-budget.sh

title: Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Why Gitea's Docker Build Ate 40 Minutes (And the 3-Line BuildKit Fix)
summary:
Notes from a 2 AM On-Call: Why Gitea's Docker Build Ate 40 Minutes (And the 3-Line BuildKit Fix)

The Failure Symptom 

Step 12/18 : RUN go mod download
 ---> Running in 3a8f9c2d1e4b
go: downloading github.com/...
[... 2,847 dependencies streaming ...]
time: 38m 42s

Our Gitea self-hosted instance CI suddenly jumped from a consistent 8-minute Docker build to 40+ minutes. No code changes. No new dependencies. Just silent, brutal layer cache misses on every single go mod download step.

GitHub Actions runner logs showed CACHE_MISS for Docker layers that should've been warm. The build worked—it just burned 32 extra minutes re-downloading the entire Go module dependency tree on every commit.

The Red Herring

Standard Docker-in-GitHub-Actions tutorials suggest:

- uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
  with:
    context: .
    cache-from: type=gha
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

We had that. Cache keys were valid. docker/setup-buildx-action was pinned. Yet Go module layers re-downloaded every time.

The actual problem? Gitea's Dockerfile had a subtle ARG ordering bug that invalidated BuildKit's layer fingerprinting.

The Root Cause

Here's the broken snippet from our Gitea fork's Dockerfile:

FROM golang:1.21-alpine AS builder

# ❌ BROKEN: ARG placed BEFORE WORKDIR
ARG GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct
ARG GITEA_VERSION=dev

WORKDIR /app
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download  # <-- This layer cache NEVER hit

Why it failed: Docker BuildKit hashes layer cache keys from the full instruction context—including ARG values and their position. When ARG GITEA_VERSION=dev appears before WORKDIR, and our CI matrix substituted it with short commit SHAs on every run (--build-arg GITEA_VERSION=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)), BuildKit saw a "new" base context and trashed the cache.

The Runnable Fix

Move the volatile ARG declarations after the stable COPY go.mod go.sum layer:

FROM golang:1.21-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /app

# ✅ FIXED: Copy dependency manifests first
COPY go.mod go.sum ./

# Now declare ARGs that change per build
ARG GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct
ARG GITEA_VERSION=dev

RUN go mod download  # <-- Cache now hits 95% of the time

Result: Build time dropped back to 7m 54s. Cache hit rate jumped from 12% to 96%.

The GitHub Actions Hardening

We also pinned BuildKit's cache backend and added explicit cache scopes to prevent cross-branch pollution:

name: Build Gitea Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  docker:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@692973e3d937129bcbf40652eb9f2f61becf3332  # v4.1.7

      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@988b5a0280414f521da01fcc63a27aeeb4b104db  # v3.6.1
        with:
          driver-opts: |
            image=moby/buildkit:v0.12.5
            network=host

      - uses: docker/build-push-action@5cd11c3a4ced054e52742c5fd54dca954e0edd85  # v6.7.0
        with:
          context: .
          push: false
          cache-from: |
            type=gha,scope=buildkit-${{ github.ref_name }}
          cache-to: |
            type=gha,mode=max,scope=buildkit-${{ github.ref_name }}
          build-args: |
            GITEA_VERSION=${{ github.sha }}
            GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct

Key changes:

  1. SHA-pinned all actions to prevent supply-chain injection.
  2. Scoped cache keys by branch (scope=buildkit-${{ github.ref_name }}) to avoid main/PR cache conflicts.
  3. Locked BuildKit image version to prevent silent backend upgrades.

Invariant Rule

In any Dockerfile intended for CI caching: Place all volatile ARG declarations (commit SHAs, build timestamps, dynamic versions) strictly AFTER the last COPY or ADD instruction that should benefit from layer reuse.

If an ARG changes on every build, treat it like a cache poison and isolate it below your stable dependency layers. BuildKit doesn't distinguish "metadata ARGs" from "build-affecting ARGs"—it just hashes the full instruction sequence.

Production Context

When we benchmarked this fix across our multi-region Gitea deployment pipeline—which fans out Docker builds to three GitHub Actions self-hosted runner pools—the aggregated CI cost dropped by 68% (measured in runner-minutes per week). We route our internal LLM-assisted code review webhooks through a relay gateway at https://b-lost.com/v1 for failover between Anthropic and OpenAI; after the build time fix, the end-to-end PR merge latency (commit → Docker build → deploy → LLM review trigger) improved from 52 minutes to under 11 minutes, keeping the review context fresh and reducing stale approval windows.

The real lesson: Docker layer cache is deterministic until it isn't. Always audit ARG placement with docker history --no-trunc and BuildKit's --progress=plain mode before blaming the registry or runner.
